label: doc_title
text: DARK CLOUD PASSES.

label: doc_title
text: BRITAIN'S COAL CRISIS SETTLED.

label: text
text: MINER'S TELEGRAM.

label: text
text: The dark cloud that has been hanging over British industry passes with the eleventh hour settlement of the coal crisis.

label: text
text: The House of Commons, crowd-d, cheered the Premier when he ntered.

label: text
text: Mr. Baldwin announced that the mine owners' notices had been suspended for a fortnight and the men had been ordered by the executive to remain at work.

label: text
text: Mr. Baldwin also stated that a provisional agreement had been reached with the mine owners, subject to district confirmation. The Miners' Executive was sending out the following telegram:—“Notices suspended — Continue working.”

label: text
text: Mr. Baldwin added that if there was any local hitch owing to the lateness of the hour at which the settlement was reached he trusted all the parties would co-operate to remove it.

label: text
text: Mr. J. R. Clynes (Labour) expressed his very great sense of relief.

label: text
text: Mr. Lloyd George (Liberal) associated himself with Mr. Clynes' words with regard to the relief felt by the whole community that this dark cloud had not at present broken upon British industry.

label: text
text: Asked with regard to the conditions reached, Mr. Baldwin said that the negotiations had only been concluded within the last five minutes. Mr. Churchill would have certain information which would be published to-night. The matter could be discussed if necessary next week, probably on Thursday.

label: paragraph_title
text: Obstacles Overcome.

label: text
text: The settlement of the coal crisis followed a series of conferences between the Premier, the parties to the dispute and the Trade Union Congress Committee.

label: text
text: It is understood the discussions in the morning related chiefly to the form and scope of the financial assistance proposed by the Government in order to bridge over the crisis and enable full investigation of the conditions of the industry.

label: text
text: A number of difficulties presented themselves, the main issue being the extent of this assistance. It is understood the owners strongly urged that Government aid should be sufficient to secure the reopening of the pits closed during the recent depression.

label: text
text:
_Mr. Cook stated that the miners wages' and conditions would continue the same until the spring or at least nine months during the sitting of the commission of enquiry into the coal industry.
The Trade Union Congress Committee circularised the trade unions announcing that the coal owners and Miners' Federation had accepted the Government proposal and the embargo on the movement of coal had been withdrawn. Work was to be continued by all the unions involved.

label: paragraph_title
text: Government's Assistance.

label: text
text:
The Government's assistance to the coal mines will take the form of subvention to aid wage for 9 months till May 1, 1926, during which wages are to be paid on the basis of the 1924 agreement, but if any month wages—calculated in accordance with the recognised ratio of division between wages and profits—are anywhere lower than the 1924 minimum the deficiency will be provided by the Exchequer, while any month in which it is estimated the average profit where the subvention is payable exceeds 1s. 5d, a ton the excess will be used in reducing the subvention. The cost involved to the Exchequer cannot at present be forecasted as it must depend on the course of trade.

COMPLAINT AGAINST MILITARY.
It is stated that twenty picked soldiers were told off to protect about three hundred people embarking by the s.s. Foo Cheong from Pakkai for Macao. Those departing were put on board small boats at Kongmoon and conveyed to the steamer where the military soon let it be known that they would brook no interference. As it was the strikers pickets could do nothing but stare and the workers sailed in peace. They will have reached Macao in due course from whence they are expected to make for Hongkong.

To day the Strike Executive announced that they would petition the Government for permission to set up their own courts of justice to try their own cases. The strikers have been keenly disappointed because men they have arrested as “enemies” and “spies” have been liberated by responsible police officials to whom they were sent for custody. label: text
text: According to a merchant from Canton, Liu Chung-oi, the present Finance Minister, is receiving about $600,000 per month from the salt revenue. Of this $400,000 is remitted to support the Whampoa Cadets, leaving $200,000 for the Treasury.

label: text
text: Liu, who has always been a labour politician, is reported in the vernacular papers to be distributing $6,000 (Canton subsidiary silver) per day to the Strike leaders for the maintenance of the strikers in Canton. This, however, is not enough. Accordingly a loan of $850,000 is being sought from private, native banks.
